Well, doctor, I... I'm here because I just can't stop thinking about my appearance. It's really taking over everything. I work as a host at this lounge downtown, you know, and the lighting in there is just... it's so harsh. It's those awful overhead spotlights they think make the place look moody and chic, but all it does is highlight everything wrong with me. I mean, my hairline, for starters. It's receding, I know it is, and under those lights, it just looks so obvious and... and my face, too. The shadows it casts, it makes my skin look sagging and weird, like I'm aging in fast forward. I look so old and strange, and I'm standing at the front door greeting people, knowing they're looking right at me. I try to tell my coworkers about it, like, "Hey, doesn't the lighting make me look terrible?" or "Look at my hairline, it's so bad today," and they always brush it off. They tell me they don't see what I'm talking about, that I look completely fine, maybe even good for 54, but I know they're just being polite. They have to be seeing it. It's right there. I spend hours before my shift just staring in the mirror, trying to fix my hair, trying to find an angle where I don't look so... grotesque. And then the whole time I'm at work, I'm just obsessing over it, wondering what the customers are thinking when they see me. It's exhausting, it really is. I just can't get it out of my head, no matter what anyone says.

Oh, it’s… it’s completely ruining it. I mean, my manager, David, he’s usually a pretty understanding guy, but he’s actually written me up. Twice now. And it’s not because I don’t know how to do my job, I’m good at my job when I’m actually there, but… I’m just late all the time. Or I call out completely. And it’s all because I get stuck at home. And it’s not just work, honestly. It’s bleeding into everything else. We used to do these staff photos, you know, for the lounge’s social media, and I used to be fine with it, but now? I refuse. I absolutely will not let them take my picture. I know how terrible I’ll look, how my face will look all saggy and old, and I can’t have that out there for everyone to see. I’ve stopped going to the gallery events downtown, too. I used to love those, but the lighting in those places is just as bad as the lounge, if not worse. And my friends… they go on these group hikes on the weekends, and I’ve just completely stopped going. I tell them I’m busy or I’m tired, but the truth is, I just can’t handle being out in the bright sunlight where everyone can see every flaw, every receding hair, every shadow on my face. I just… I can’t handle being seen that way anymore. It’s just too much.

I don't think it does. I mean, it's always the hairline, always the face. It's not like I wake up on a Tuesday and suddenly I'm worried about my nose or my ears, you know? It's always this same, heavy dread about the receding hair and the sagging skin. \n\nBut I guess... I guess I haven't really tracked it day by day in a journal or anything. I just know that every single morning, it's the same routine. I get up, I walk into the bathroom, I turn on the light, and boom—there it is. The hairline. The shadows. It feels like the same exact nightmare playing on a loop. But as for whether the intensity of it shifts, or if the exact angle of the sag bothers me more one day than the next... I couldn't really say for sure. I just know it's always there, always ruining my day, always making me dread walking into that lounge. It's just a constant, heavy weight, doctor. I don't know if that answers your question, but it's just... it's always those same things, just dragging me down.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think that maybe your coworkers are telling the truth when they say they don't see these flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: I mean... I want to believe them. I really, really do. Sometimes I’ll be standing at the host podium, and one of the bartenders—like Sarah, she’s this very sweet girl, always trying to keep morale up—she’ll tell me, you know, \"You’re crazy, you look perfectly fine.\" And for a split second, maybe just a fraction of a second, I try to convince myself that maybe she’s telling the truth. Maybe I am just being too hard on myself. \n\nBut then... then I catch my reflection in the glass of the front door, or I have to walk a menu over to a table under one of those overhead pendant lights. And the moment that light hits me, all of Sarah's reassurance just completely evaporates. It's just gone. Because I'm staring right at it. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes. Yes, I have. And it’s… it’s actually becoming a huge problem, to be perfectly honest with you. It’s affecting everything. I mean, at work, at the lounge, I’ve actually been written up recently. Which is so humiliating, because I’ve always prided myself on being a reliable employee, you know? But I’ve been late so many times lately, or I’ve just straight-up missed shifts entirely. And it’s not because I don’t want to work or because I overslept. It’s because I’ll be in the bathroom, trying to fix my hair, trying to get the part just right so it doesn’t look so horribly receded, or I’ll be staring at my face, dreading walking under those amber pendant lights I told you about. And the time just slips away. I’ll spend an hour, two hours, just frozen there, trying to fix something that can’t be fixed, and before I know it, I’m an hour late for my shift. Or I get so overwhelmed by how hideous I look that I just call out sick. I just can’t bring myself to walk out the front door and let people see me looking so old and strange.

And it’s not just work, either. It’s my personal life, too. It’s completely shrinking. We used to do these staff photos at the lounge—you know, they like to post them on the restaurant’s Instagram to show off the "team culture" or whatever—and I absolutely refuse to participate anymore. I just step out of the frame or go hide in the back room until they’re done. The thought of my face and my hairline being permanently captured and put on the internet for everyone to scrutinize… I can’t handle it. I’d have a panic attack. 

And outside of work, I used to love going to gallery events downtown. There’s this great little art community here, and I used to go to openings on my nights off. But the lighting in those galleries is always so stark, so bright and unforgiving. I went to one a few months ago and caught a glimpse of myself in a mirrored sculpture, and I swear, my skin looked so hollow and sagging I practically ran out of the building. I haven’t been back to a gallery since. I don’t even go on the weekend group hikes I used to do with some friends. You’d think hiking would be fine, right? You’re outside, wearing a hat maybe. But no, the sun beats down, and it creates these harsh shadows on my face, and I just know everyone is looking at me, thinking about how much I’ve aged, how terrible I look. So I just make up excuses. I tell them I pulled a muscle or I have to work. But the truth is, I just can’t bear the thought of being seen. It’s like I’m hiding from the world because I’m so ashamed of what I look like.

I mean... is it possible? I guess... I mean, theoretically, anything is possible in the grand scheme of things, right? But... no. Not really. When I look in the mirror, it’s the first thing my eyes go to, and it just feels like it’s getting worse every single day. I’ll stand there and comb it this way and that way, trying to see if maybe a part on the left hides it better, or maybe if I use a little more product it won’t look so thin, but it never works. It just looks like this glaring beacon of... of aging and ugliness. \n\nAnd then there’s my face. It’s the way my face looks, especially under those terrible lights at the lounge. It’s like the shadows just pool in all the wrong places, you know? It makes my skin look saggy and hollow, and it just makes me look so incredibly old and strange. Like a caricature of myself. I’ll be standing at the host stand, and the overhead spotlight is just beating down on me, and I can literally feel how bad I look. I can feel the shadows on my face. And I try to talk to my coworkers about it—I’ll say, \"Look at my hairline today, it’s a disaster,\" or \"This lighting makes my face look so sunken, doesn't it?\" And they just look at me like I’m crazy. They tell me they don’t see what I’m talking about, that my hair looks fine, that my face looks completely normal. They say, \"You look great for 54, stop worrying!\" But I know they’re just saying that to be nice, or maybe they just don’t want to deal with me. Because how could they not see it? It’s right there. I can’t stop thinking about it, doctor. It’s just this constant, looping thought in my head—my hairline, my face, how old and strange I look, and how everyone must be staring at it, even if they pretend they aren't. It just consumes me.\n\nDoctor: Do your concerns about your appearance stay the same or do they change from day to day?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, it's... it's interesting you ask that, because I've thought about this a lot. I mean, when I'm standing there in the bathroom, staring in the mirror, sometimes I wonder if I'm just hyper-fixating on one thing, but... honestly, I don't really know if it changes. I don't think it does. I mean, it's always the hairline, always the face. It's not like I wake up on a Tuesday and suddenly I'm worried about my nose or my ears, you know? It's always this same, heavy dread about the receding hair and the sagging skin. \n\nBut I guess... I guess I haven't really tracked it day by day in a journal or anything. I just know that every single morning, it's the same routine. I get up, I walk into the bathroom, I turn on the light, and boom—there it is. The hairline. The shadows. I couldn't really say for sure. I just know it's always there, always ruining my day, always making me dread walking into that lounge. It's just a constant, heavy weight, doctor. I can't turn the thoughts off, even when they tell me they don't see it. It’s like we are looking at two completely different realities, and I just... And it’s not because I don’t want to work or because I overslept. It’s like I’m hiding from the world because I’m so ashamed of what I look like.\n\nDoctor: Are there any other areas of your life, besides work and social events, where your concerns about your appearance are causing you problems?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly... That was just devastating for me. They say, \"You look great for 54, stop worrying!\" But I know they’re just saying that to be nice, or maybe they just don’t want to deal with me. Because how could they not see it? It’s right there. I can’t stop thinking about it, doctor. It’s just this constant, looping thought in my head—my hairline, my face, how old and strange I look, and how everyone must be staring at it, even if they pretend they aren't. It just consumes me.\n\nDoctor: Do your concerns about your appearance stay the same or do they change from day to day?\n\nPatient: Well, you know, it's... it's interesting you ask that, because I've thought about this a lot. I mean, when I'm standing there in the bathroom, staring in the mirror, sometimes I wonder if I'm just hyper-fixating on one thing, but... honestly, I don't really know if it changes. I don't think it does. I mean, it's always the hairline, always the face. It's not like I wake up on a Tuesday and suddenly I'm worried about my nose or my ears, you know? It's always this same, heavy dread about the receding hair and the sagging skin. \n\nBut I guess... I guess I haven't really tracked it day by day in a journal or anything. I just know that every single morning, it's the same routine. I get up, I walk into the bathroom, I turn on the light, and boom—there it is. The hairline. The shadows. It feels like the same exact nightmare playing on a loop. But as for whether the intensity of it shifts, or if the exact angle of the sag bothers me more one day than the next... I couldn't really say for sure. I just know it's always there, always ruining my day, always making me dread walking into that lounge. It's just a constant, heavy weight, doctor. I don't know if that answers your question, but it's just... it's always those same things, just dragging me down.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever think that maybe your coworkers are telling the truth when they say they don't see these flaws in your appearance?\n\nPatient: I mean... Maybe I am just being too hard on myself. \n\nBut then... then I catch my reflection in the glass of the front door, or I have to walk a menu over to a table under one of those overhead pendant lights. I mean... I hear what you're saying. I do. And part of me knows that, technically speaking, I'm 54 years old, and people age. I understand the biology of it. But... no. No, I don't think it's just an exaggerated concern. Because if it were just normal aging, why would it be taking over my entire life? 

I know I’ve brought this up over and over again today—and I apologize for sounding like a broken record, I really do, but it’s just... it’s the whole reason I finally made this appointment. I’m sitting here because I literally cannot stop thinking about it. It’s not just a passing thought of, "Oh, I'm getting a little older." It is a constant, suffocating obsession. I can’t stop thinking about my hairline, the way it’s receding so drastically, and the way my face looks... especially under those specific lights at the restaurant. I mean, the lighting in the lounge is supposed to be flattering, all dim and amber, but somehow it just catches every single shadow, every bit of sagging, and it just makes me look so incredibly old and... and strange. Bizarre, even. 

And look, I know my coworkers tell me I’m crazy. I know they say they don’t see what I’m talking about. We’ll be standing by the host stand, waiting for the dinner rush, and I’ll try to point it out—just subtly, you know, asking if the overhead spot is making me look weird—and they always brush it off. "You look fine," they say. "You look like you." But how can I believe them when I see what I see in the mirror? When I feel the way people look at me when they walk in the door? 

If it were just normal, if I were just within the "normal range" for my age, I wouldn't be spending hours locked in my bathroom before a shift, physically unable to leave my house because I'm trying to fix something that can't be fixed. I wouldn't be getting written up at a job I've held together for years. I wouldn't have abandoned my entire social life, my Sunday hikes, my friends... all of it. So, no, doctor, I don't think it's exaggerated. I think it's very real, and I think it's ruining my life, and I just... I can't turn my brain off from it. I just can't stop thinking about how strange I look.

Because—and I know I keep circling back to this, I know I’m probably driving you crazy saying the exact same thing over and over, but I really need you to understand—I am sitting here in this office today specifically because I just cannot stop thinking about it. But even if they don't, it doesn't change anything for me, you know? It doesn't turn the thoughts off. I'm still trapped in my own head, completely fixated on it. I simply cannot reconcile what they are saying with what my own two eyes are showing me every single day. \n\nI stand there in front of the mirror, sometimes for hours on end, and I study every single millimeter of my hairline. I see the exact depth of the shadows on my face. I see the sagging. It's physical. It's tangible. It's right there in front of me. So when you ask if my perception is different from how others actually see me... I mean, honestly, I think maybe they're just not paying close attention. People are busy, you know? Especially at the lounge. They walk in, they glance at you, they ask for a table, they order their drinks, and they move on with their evening. They aren't studying me under those amber pendant lights the way I have to. They aren't seeing the harsh reality of how old and strange I look because they just aren't looking that closely at me. They have their own lives to worry about. \n\nSo, no, I really don't think my perception is skewed or different or whatever. I think I'm just the only one who is forced to really, truly look at the reality of it. I'm the one who has to live in this body and see the truth of it in every reflection, every window, every mirrored sculpture. And it's exhausting, it really, truly is, but I can't just pretend I don't see what is so clearly right there in front of my face. I wish I could, doctor, I really do, but I just can't.\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's any possibility that your appearance is not as flawed as you perceive it to be?\n\nPatient: I mean, we sort of just touched on this, but... no. I really don't think there's a possibility it's less flawed than I see it. The whole reason I’m even sitting here in this office talking to you today is exactly because I just can’t stop thinking about it. It is a constant, endless loop in my head. I’m here because I am entirely consumed by the fact that my hairline and the way my face looks, especially under those harsh restaurant lights at the lounge, make me look so incredibly old and strange. \n\nAnd I know my coworkers tell me they don’t see what I’m talking about. Just the other night, one of the bartenders caught me checking my reflection in the side of the espresso machine, and he told me I looked completely fine and that I was worrying over nothing. But how can he say that? How can any of them say that? They just wave it off. I try to explain it to them, I try to point out exactly where the recession is happening on my scalp, exactly how the shadows from those amber pendant lights pool under my eyes and make my skin look all saggy and bizarre, but they just dismiss it. They tell me I am making a mountain out of a molehill. \n\nBut it is not a molehill. If it were just some minor little thing, I wouldn't be missing my shifts, you know? I wouldn't be agonizing over it every single waking minute of the day. It is literally all I can focus on. I wake up thinking about it, I go to sleep dreading the next day because of it. So when you ask if maybe it is not as bad as I think... I just keep coming back to the fact that I cannot turn off these thoughts. I cannot stop seeing how old and strange I look, no matter how many times the people at work tell me they don't see what I am talking about. It is just completely consuming me, doctor, it really, truly is.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your concerns about your appearance are significantly interfering with your ability to enjoy life or function normally?\n\nPatient: Well, yes... absolutely. I mean, I know I’ve already touched on this a bit today, but... yes, it is completely ruining my ability to function. I mean, I’m barely functioning at all. Like I was saying earlier about the restaurant... getting written up? You have to understand how incredibly out of character that is for me. I’m 54 years old. I’ve always prided myself on being the reliable one, the person who holds the floor together. But now? I’m getting these formal warnings because I’m chronically late, or I just completely miss my shifts. And it’s not because I don’t care about my job! It’s because I get stuck in my bathroom for hours, just paralyzed, trying to fix myself or just agonizing over the mirror, and I physically cannot walk out the door. How do you explain that to a manager? You can't. \n\nAnd as for enjoying life... there is just no joy left. None. I mentioned the gallery events downtown and the weekend hikes... I used to absolutely live for those. There was this one trail we’d do every Sunday morning, and we'd all go grab coffee afterward, and it was just a wonderful community. But I’ve completely stopped going to all of it. I haven't been in months. I just can’t stomach the thought of them seeing me out there in the harsh daylight, sweating, with my face and my hairline looking the way they do. \n\nAnd those staff photos I brought up? They were doing a whole new website rollout for the lounge, bringing in a professional photographer, and I just flat-out refused to go. I called in sick that day, too. I just... I simply cannot handle being seen that way, by anyone. So, yes, to answer your question, it's interfering with everything. It has completely dismantled my life. I don't even know what a normal day looks like anymore, because my entire existence is just trying to avoid being looked at.\n\nDoctor: Do you think someone who didn't know you, a stranger, would notice the flaws in your appearance that you're concerned about?\n\nPatient: I mean... yes. I think about it constantly. \n\nEvery single time the front door opens and a new party walks in, my heart just drops into my stomach because I know, I just *know* they are noticing the recession, the sagging, the shadows. It’s the very first thing they see. I just can't turn off the thought that these people, these total strangers, are looking at me and judging how bizarre my face looks the absolute second they lay eyes on me. So, yes, a stranger would absolutely notice. How could they not?\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if I were to look at you right now, I would see the same flaws in your appearance that you're describing?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean... yes. I really do. I know you're a doctor and you're supposed to be objective and everything, but you have eyes, right? You're sitting right there, looking straight at me. And I know I keep coming back to this, I know I've said it a dozen times already since I sat down, but it's the whole reason I'm here... I just cannot stop thinking about it. It's this constant, overwhelming preoccupation. I'm here because I am so consumed by the fact that my hairline is receding the way it is, and the way my face just looks so... so old and strange. \n\nAnd I know, I know I've told you that the people I work with at the lounge, the bartenders and the servers, they tell me they don't see what I'm talking about. They say I look fine. But like I said, they're used to me, or they're just being nice. But you? You're looking at me right now, in this lighting—which, by the way, is a lot brighter and more clinical than the amber lights at the restaurant—and I just know you have to see it. How could you not? You're looking right at my forehead, right at the way the skin sags. It's impossible to hide. So, yes, if you're really looking at me, really observing me the way a doctor does, I absolutely believe you see the exact same flaws I've been describing this whole time. I just... I can't imagine anyone looking at me and not seeing exactly what I see every time I look in the mirror.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your appearance is actually within the normal range for someone of your age, but your concern about it is exaggerated?\n\nPatient: I mean... I hear what you're saying. I do. And part of me knows that, technically speaking, I'm 54 years old, and people age. I understand the biology of it. But... no. But I’ve completely stopped going to all of it. I haven't been in months. I just can’t stomach the thought of them seeing me out there in the harsh daylight, sweating, with my face and my hairline looking the way they do. \n\nAnd those staff photos I brought up? They were doing a whole new website rollout for the lounge, bringing in a professional photographer, and I just flat-out refused to go. I called in sick that day, too. I just... I simply cannot handle being seen that way, by anyone. So, yes, to answer your question, it's interfering with everything. It has completely dismantled my life. I don't even know what a normal day looks like anymore, because my entire existence is just trying to avoid being looked at.\n\nDoctor: Do you think someone who didn't know you, a stranger, would notice the flaws in your appearance that you're concerned about?\n\nPatient: I mean... yes. Absolutely. A stranger? I honestly think a stranger would notice it even faster than anyone else. When someone walks into the lounge for the first time, they don't have any preconceived notions of me, you know? They just see what's right there in front of them. And like I keep saying—and I know I keep hammering on this, but it is literally the entire reason I am sitting in this chair today—I just cannot stop thinking about my hairline and the way my face looks. It’s a constant, never-ending loop in my brain. \n\nI know I told you my coworkers claim they don't see what I'm talking about, but they see me every single day. They’re used to me. Or, you know, maybe they're just being polite because we have to work together and they don't want to make things awkward during a busy shift. But a stranger walking in off the street? They're going to look at the host stand and immediately see exactly how old and strange I look under those restaurant lights. I think about it constantly. \n\nEvery single time the front door opens and a new party walks in, my heart just drops into my stomach because I know, I just *know* they are noticing the recession, the sagging, the shadows. It’s the very first thing they see. I just can't turn off the thought that these people, these total strangers, are looking at me and judging how bizarre my face looks the absolute second they lay eyes on me. So, yes, a stranger would absolutely notice. How could they not?\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if I were to look at you right now, I would see the same flaws in your appearance that you're describing?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean... yes. I really do. I know you're a doctor and you're supposed to be objective and everything, but you have eyes, right? You're sitting right there, looking straight at me. And I know I keep coming back to this, I know I've said it a dozen times already since I sat down, but it's the whole reason I'm here... I just cannot stop thinking about it. It's this constant, overwhelming preoccupation. I'm here because I am so consumed by the fact that my hairline is receding the way it is, and the way my face just looks so... so old and strange. \n\nAnd I know, I know I've told you that the people I work with at the lounge, the bartenders and the servers, they tell me they don't see what I'm talking about. So, yes, if you're really looking at me, really observing me the way a doctor does, I absolutely believe you see the exact same flaws I've been describing this whole time. I just... I can't imagine anyone looking at me and not seeing exactly what I see every time I look in the mirror.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your appearance is actually within the normal range for someone of your age, but your concern about it is exaggerated?\n\nPatient: I mean... I hear what you're saying. I do. And part of me knows that, technically speaking, I'm 54 years old, and people age. I understand the biology of it. But... no. No, I don't think it's just an exaggerated concern. Because if it were just normal aging, why would it be taking over my entire life? \n\nI know I’ve brought this up over and over again today—and I apologize for sounding like a broken record, I really do, but it’s just... it’s the whole reason I finally made this appointment. I’m sitting here because I literally cannot stop thinking about it. It’s not just a passing thought of, \"Oh, I'm getting a little older.\" It is a constant, suffocating obsession. I can’t stop thinking about my hairline, the way it’s receding so drastically, and the way my face looks... especially under those specific lights at the restaurant. We’ll be standing by the host stand, waiting for the dinner rush, and I’ll try to point it out—just subtly, you know, asking if the overhead spot is making me look weird—and they always brush it off. \"You look fine,\" they say. \"You look like you.\" But how can I believe them when I see what I see in the mirror? When I feel the way people look at me when they walk in the door? \n\nIf it were just normal, if I were just within the \"normal range\" for my age, I wouldn't be spending hours locked in my bathroom before a shift, physically unable to leave my house because I'm trying to fix something that can't be fixed. I wouldn't be getting written up at a job I've held together for years. I wouldn't have abandoned my entire social life, my Sunday hikes, my friends... all of it. So, no, doctor, I don't think it's exaggerated. I think it's very real, and I think it's ruining my life, and I just... I can't turn my brain off from it. I just can't stop thinking about how strange I look.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your appearance is not as flawed as you think it is, and that others see you differently than you see yourself?\n\nPatient: I mean... I suppose, theoretically, it’s possible. I try to tell myself that sometimes. But... I just don't know how to actually believe it. Because—and I know I keep circling back to this, I know I’m probably driving you crazy saying the exact same thing over and over, but I really need you to understand—I am sitting here in this office today specifically because I just cannot stop thinking about it. So even if it is possible that I'm not as flawed as I think I am... it doesn't matter, because I can't see it. I can't escape the thought that I look completely strange. It's just... it's always there, playing on a loop.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your perception of your flaws is not based in reality?\n\nPatient: Reality... I mean, that’s a heavy word, isn't it? Reality. I try to wrap my head around what you're asking, I really do. Am I completely disconnected from reality? I don't feel like I am. I feel like I'm seeing exactly what is physically right there in front of me in the mirror. But then... I don't know, maybe my reality is just broken. Because, and I know I am beating a dead horse here, I know I have said this to you so many times already today, but it is literally the entire reason I am sitting here in your office. I am here because I just cannot stop thinking about it. It is this constant, endless loop in my brain that my hairline is just gone, and the way my face looks... especially when I am at work, standing right under those restaurant lights, it just makes me look so profoundly old and strange. \n\nAnd you bring up reality, and it makes me think about what my coworkers say. Like I told you, they tell me they don’t see what I’m talking about. The bartenders, the other staff, they look at me and swear that I look normal, that I am obsessing over things that aren't even there. So I guess, if you look at it from their perspective, maybe my perception isn't based in their reality. But how am I supposed to live in their reality when I am completely trapped in mine? \n\nEven when they promise me that I look fine, it doesn't change anything in my head. I’m still standing at the host stand, smiling at customers, handing out menus, and the entire time I am completely paralyzed by the thought of how bizarre my face looks in that specific lighting. I can feel the shadows on my sagging skin. So whether it is based in objective, biological reality or not... the obsession is real. The fact that I can't stop thinking about it for even a single minute of my shift, that is my reality. I just can't escape it, no matter who tells me I'm wrong.\n\nDoctor: Is there a particular part of your body that you're most concerned about?\n\nPatient: Well, like I’ve been saying—and I know I’ve brought this up in basically every answer so far, and I really do apologize for dominating the conversation with it, but it’s just the absolute core of why I’m here—it’s my hairline. It’s just... it’s my face, Doctor. My hair and my face. I am completely consumed by how bizarre they look under those lights, and I just can't turn the thoughts off, no matter what anyone says to me.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your appearance is completely normal, but your brain is just making you think it's not?\n\nPatient: I... I just can't make myself believe it. \n\nBecause—and I know I am a broken record today, I know I just keep coming back to this exact same point, but it's the only thing that matters—I am sitting here talking to you right now because I cannot stop the thoughts.
